did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter mentions Haggai and Zechariah as prophets who prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel.

Did you know? In response to the prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak began rebuilding the house of God in Jerusalem, and the prophets supported them.
Did you know? Tattenai, governor of Trans-Euphrates, Shethar-Bozenai, and their associates asked the builders who had given them permission to build the house and restore the structure.

Did you know? Although the officials questioned the construction, they did not stop it; according to the text, the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, and the matter was referred to Darius for a decision.
Did you know? Tattenai, Shethar-Bozenai, and their associates sent Darius an official letter concerning the construction of the house of God in Jerusalem.

Did you know? The letter to Darius states that the house of God was being built with large stones and that wooden beams were being laid in the walls; it also says that the work was progressing successfully.
Did you know? The elders of the Jews identified themselves as servants of the God of heaven and earth, and said that the temple had formerly been built by a great king of Israel.

Did you know? According to the elders’ reply, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree in his first year to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem, after the temple had been destroyed and the people exiled in the days of Nebuchadnezzar.

Did you know? The gold and silver temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and brought to Babylon were returned in the days of Cyrus and entrusted to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor.

Did you know? At the end of the letter, Tattenai and his associates asked Darius to search the royal archives in Babylon to determine whether Cyrus had indeed issued a decree to build the house of God in Jerusalem.
